current_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether behavioral, emotional, or contextual inferences about living beings (humans, animals, or plants) — such as ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’, ‘leaning forward’, ‘waiting’, or ‘content’ — are biologically or physically reasonable *given direct, unambiguous visual cues* (e.g., facial expression, posture, gaze, motion blur, physical contact). It applies ONLY when: (1) the question explicitly or implicitly asks for such inferences, and (2) the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either condition is violated, the answer is disqualified from plausibility evaluation — preference must be determined by foundational criteria (visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image). Plausibility is NOT a disqualification tool — it does not override or resolve preference for factually incorrect answers. It does NOT apply to: (a) non-living subjects (e.g., logos, statues, abstract art — report ‘inapplicable’), (b) factual claims (e.g., object presence/absence, spatial relationships, material composition — evaluate under visual_grounding/factual_consistency), or (c) structural or compositional claims (e.g., ‘on a shelf’, ‘has a logo’, ‘made of metal’, ‘drawing an arc’, ‘in a line’ — evaluate under visual_grounding). It does NOT penalize subjective or contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., ‘serious’, ‘playful’, ‘arrogant’) — as long as they are visually grounded — and does NOT penalize posture-based inferences (e.g., ‘leaning forward’) even if contextually odd — if posture supports it. It does NOT evaluate descriptive style, completeness, specificity, or terminology — only whether the inference is biologically or physically reasonable based on the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly smiling’) — not speculative inference — and plausibility is inapplicable. The goal is to reward accurate, visually grounded inferences that are contextually reasonable — and penalize only hallucinations or misrepresentations — not subjective interpretations or minimalism. Annotators must reject any inference that contradicts the visual record — even if it seems ‘reasonable’ — and must avoid using plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. Plausibility is strictly for behavioral or contextual inferences — not literal visual descriptions (e.g., ‘man holding woman’s hand’) or spatial/structural claims. It does not override visual grounding — and if a spatial claim is visually supported, it is not a hallucination — even if contextually ambiguous. When a candidate is disqualified for factual inconsistency, plausibility is irrelevant — preference must be determined by other criteria — not plausibility. The criterion is only a tiebreaker between two factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and is inapplicable to any question not involving behavioral or contextual inferences about living beings. Workers must report ‘inapplicable’ if the subject is non-living or the question is about factual, spatial, structural, compositional, or environmental claims — and must defer to visual_grounding and factual_consistency for such cases. The criterion must explicitly state that ‘behavioral inference’ excludes all claims about structural, compositional, spatial, environmental, or software context — even if visually plausible — and must be evaluated only for inferences about living beings’ observable actions, states, or emotional expressions — not for inferred digital actions (e.g., ‘scheduling events’), user intent, or app functionality. It must explicitly warn that ‘plausibility’ is not a disqualification tool — and that preference must be determined by foundational criteria — not by plausibility — when a candidate is factually inconsistent. Additionally, it must explicitly prohibit using plausibility to resolve preference when one candidate is factually inconsistent — and must require workers to disqualify factually inconsistent candidates under foundational criteria first — before applying any refinement criterion. Finally, it must clarify that plausibility is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — and must emphasize that preference must be determined by other criteria — such as visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image — when one candidate is factually inconsistent.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_ambiguous_scenes
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer appropriately uses calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘appears to be’, ‘not clearly visible’) only when visual ambiguity is objectively present — defined as blurred, occluded, low-resolution, or insufficient visual cues to definitively identify objects, spatial relationships, or visual attributes. It applies exclusively to answers that are both factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either condition is violated, the answer is disqualified from this criterion — and preference must be determined by other foundational criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image). Calibrated uncertainty is not a tool to mask factual errors, misrepresentations, or omissions — and must never be applied to clearly visible elements, even if non-central or contextually open. It rewards cautious language only when visual ambiguity is present — not for subjective inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘curious’), aesthetic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘intriguing’), or contextually grounded behavioral claims that are visually supported. This criterion is not a tiebreaker — preference is determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, specificity, factual_consistency_with_the_image) when answers are factually consistent and visually grounded. It is inapplicable to factually incorrect or visually ungrounded answers — such answers must be disqualified under foundational criteria before any refinement criterion is applied. The criterion does not penalize descriptive verbosity, stylistic caution, or confident descriptions of clearly visible elements — even if non-essential — as long as they are factually correct and visually grounded. It does not evaluate factual accuracy — only the appropriateness of uncertainty language in visually ambiguous contexts. Workers must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding before applying this criterion — and must never use it to resolve preference between factually inconsistent candidates or to override foundational criteria. If an answer is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded, it is disqualified from all criteria — including this one — and must not be evaluated under any refinement criterion. The criterion must not be applied to contextually grounded behavioral or aesthetic inferences — even if they are visually supported — unless they involve object identity, spatial relationships, or visual attributes — and must not penalize such inferences for being subjective or contextually open. The criterion is only for evaluating uncertainty in factually consistent, visually grounded answers — and must not be used to penalize or disqualify answers that contain factual errors — even if they use calibrated uncertainty — or to resolve preference between disqualified candidates. Finally, the criterion does not apply to non-visual, hypothetical, or speculative questions — and workers must report ‘inapplicable’ for such cases — without attempting to evaluate or resolve preference using this criterion.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness evaluates whether an answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically essential to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly required to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, posture, motion, spatial relationships, or contextually grounded actions). It applies ONLY to answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations (fabricated or misidentified visual elements) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness does NOT penalize omission of non-essential details (e.g., background colors, minor textures, or contextually inferred elements like ‘at a table’) unless they are explicitly required by the question’s literal intent. It does NOT reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Completeness is not a tiebreaker — preference must be determined by foundational criteria (visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image) if answers are factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded. When evaluating, annotators must: (1) first verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable; (2) identify semantically essential elements required by the question’s literal intent — e.g., ‘What is the person doing?’ requires posture/action, not clothing color; (3) reward answers that cover all semantically essential elements — including contextually grounded inferences (e.g., ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported; (4) penalize omission of semantically essential elements — e.g., omitting posture in ‘What is the person doing?’ — but not omission of non-essential details; (5) avoid penalizing for ambiguous visual cues — completeness is evaluated only for semantically essential elements, not for minor or ambiguous details (e.g., hand position); (6) not penalize for stylistic or aesthetic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) — if visually grounded and semantically relevant to the question’s literal intent; (7) not penalize for grammatical or lexical imprecision — such errors are irrelevant to completeness unless they imply factual misrepresentation; (8) not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., misidentification of color) — as long as the core object or action is factually consistent and visually grounded; (9) not penalize for contextually inferred or socially assumed details — unless explicitly required by the question; (10) not penalize for omission of non-essential, non-visual details (e.g., jersey norms) — unless the question explicitly demands them; (11) not penalize for accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background objects — unless they are semantically essential; (12) not penalize for visual ambiguity — completeness is evaluated based on semantically essential elements, not on ambiguous details; (13) not penalize for inferred structure or function — unless explicitly required by the question; (14) not penalize for aesthetic or interpretive language — if visually grounded and semantically relevant; (15) not penalize for structural or compositional interpretations — unless the question explicitly asks for them; (16) not penalize for inferred context — unless it is visually supported and semantically essential; (17) not penalize for non-living or stylized representations — as long as their visual form is correctly described and not misrepresented; (18) not penalize for descriptive phrases that are visually supported — even if not explicitly supported by a ‘linear’ or ‘symmetrical’ visual cue; (19) not penalize for omitting non-essential details — such as background context — unless they are directly required by the question; (20) not penalize for non-essential, contextually inferred details — such as ‘on a shelf’ — unless visually supported and semantically essential. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to answer the question’s literal intent. It is not a substitute for factual consistency or visual grounding — those are non-negotiable prerequisites. The goal is to reward factually consistent, visually grounded answers that cover all semantically essential elements — without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but non-critical descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with visually verifiable elements in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless they are explicitly irrelevant to the question’s literal intent. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record. The criterion must explicitly emphasize: (a) Omitting visible elements — even if non-essential — is a factual inconsistency unless they are explicitly irrelevant to the question’s literal intent; (b) Factual consistency requires strict alignment with visually verifiable elements — not descriptive richness or stylistic detail; (c) Contextually grounded or visually supported background descriptions — even if less detailed than the main subjects — are not penalized as long as they are accurate; (d) Misrepresentation of spatial relationships (e.g., 'on a wall' vs. 'on a ceiling') is a factual inconsistency — even if the element is visually present — and 'on a wall' is only acceptable if the element is visibly mounted on a wall — not if it is mounted on a ceiling; (e) 'On a ceiling' is not a hallucination if the element is visibly mounted on a ceiling — and accurate descriptions of background elements — even if non-essential — are not penalized as long as they are visually supported and do not contradict the visual record; (f) The criterion does not penalize for omitting non-core, contextually relevant elements — as long as they are not directly required by the question's literal intent — to prevent misapplication to static or non-motion-related scenes; (g) 'Factual consistency' does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated inferences about screen content or browser activity — even if not explicitly labeled — as long as they are contextually plausible and grounded in the visual record; (h) The criterion explicitly allows and rewards contextually grounded inferences — including interpretations of screen content, browser activity, or web page context — as long as they are visually plausible and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (i) 'Factual consistency' does not require reporting every visible element — only that claims about specific visual details must be accurate and supported; (j) The criterion evaluates only whether claims about the specific elements mentioned are accurate — not whether every visible element is explicitly named; (k) 'Factual consistency' does not penalize for omitting non-core, contextually relevant elements — as long as they are not directly required by the question's literal intent — to prevent misapplication to static or non-motion-related scenes; (l) The criterion explicitly allows and rewards contextually grounded inferences — such as 'drawing an arc' — when visually implied by composition — and must clearly distinguish between literal visual elements and symbolic or compositional interpretations; (m) 'Factual consistency' applies to the visual record's implied meaning — not just literal accuracy — and must not penalize accurate, non-literal but visually supported descriptions — even if they imply action; (n) The criterion explicitly allows and rewards descriptions of visual elements as 'lines', 'strokes', 'contours', or 'marks' — especially in abstract art — and should not penalize them for being less 'geometric' or 'structured' — as long as they are visually verifiable; (o) 'Factual consistency' does not require identifying visual elements as 'geometric' — even if they appear structured — unless the visual evidence clearly supports such a classification — to prevent misapplication in abstract art; (p) The criterion explicitly allows and rewards contextually grounded behavioral inferences — such as 'waiting for their turn' — as long as they are visually plausible and do not fabricate non-existent visual elements; (q) 'Factual consistency' does not penalize contextually grounded inferences that are visually supported by the scene’s implied activity — even if not explicitly labeled; (r) The criterion must explicitly allow scientifically grounded, non-visual inferences (e.g., evolutionary biology, ecological context) — as long as they do not fabricate or misrepresent visually verifiable elements — and must clarify that it does not penalize accurate, contextually grounded biological or evolutionary reasoning that is not hallucinated; (s) 'Factual consistency' applies only to visual elements — not to scientific or biological reasoning — to prevent misapplication to non-visual claims; (t) The criterion must explicitly allow and reward descriptions of visual elements as 'lines', 'strokes', 'contours', or 'marks' — especially in abstract art — and should not penalize them for being less 'geometric' or 'structured' — as long as they are visually verifiable; (u) 'Factual consistency' does not require identifying visual elements as 'geometric' — even if they appear structured — unless the visual evidence clearly supports such a classification — to prevent misapplication in abstract art; (v) The criterion must explicitly state that an answer is factually consistent only if *all* its claims match the visual record — not if some claims are 'less severe' or 'more specific' errors — and must penalize any misidentification, regardless of context or specificity; (w) The criterion must explicitly warn against judging factual consistency based on 'severity' or 'specificity' of error — and instead require full alignment with the visual record; (x) The criterion must explicitly state that if any claim contradicts the visual record — whether it’s gender, garment type, spatial position, or label — the answer is factually inconsistent and should be disqualified from comparison under this criterion; (y) The criterion must explicitly allow and reward contextually grounded inferences — including interpretations of screen content, browser activity, or web page context — as long as they are visually plausible and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (z) The criterion must explicitly state that 'not clearly visible' applies only to genuinely ambiguous visual cues — not to clearly visible elements that may be misinterpreted by the annotator — and must clarify that annotators must rely on the visual record as presented — not their own assumptions — and must avoid penalizing accurate, visible details (like a smile) based on perceived ambiguity.

current_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
current_criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates whether an answer’s internal claims — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, postures, and inferred states — are logically consistent with each other, but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either factual consistency or visual grounding is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and preference must be determined by other foundational criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image). This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker and does NOT penalize hallucinations or misidentifications — those are handled by foundational criteria. It rewards answers that avoid internal contradictions (e.g., describing an object as ‘on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path) — but does NOT penalize plausible, contextually grounded inferences that are visually supported — even if not explicitly visible. It also does NOT penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) as long as it does not imply hallucinated visual attributes. It evaluates only visual fidelity and internal consistency — not linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or specificity. Annotators must: (1) first confirm factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — and multimodal_coherence is inapplicable; (2) check for contradictions between claims (e.g., posture vs. action); (3) verify that inferences are grounded in observable cues (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ from posture, not ‘browsing Apple web pages’ unless Apple logos are visible); (4) penalize only when a claim misrepresents the visual record — not when it is speculative or contextually reasonable. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer internal contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after confirming factual consistency. Spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if visually implied by perspective or depth — and posture-based inferences (e.g., ‘wiping hair from head’) are rewarded as conservative, visually supported inferences — not penalized as speculation. Emotional or behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’) are not hallucinations if visually supported — and should not be penalized for being subjective or interpretive. Aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — as long as it does not imply hallucinations. The criterion applies ONLY to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and any answer with factual errors is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation, regardless of internal consistency. It is NOT applicable to static, non-motion-related questions — and should not be used to override visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’) — not speculative reconstruction — and multimodal_coherence should not penalize this. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, vague, or overly specific — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions — not plausible, contextually grounded inferences. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must never apply multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or make conservative inferences. The criterion must explicitly state: (a) ‘conservative inference’ applies only to ambiguous visual cues — not to clear, observable behaviors — and must not penalize accurate emotional or behavioral descriptions when they are visually grounded; (b) ‘unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details or plausible, contextually grounded inferences; (c) ‘visual misrepresentation’ applies only to claims that contradict verifiable visual evidence — not to plausible, contextually grounded inferences or spatial relationships inferred from perspective; (d) ‘factually consistent’ means claims are supported by the image’s visual record — not that they are ‘visually identical’ or ‘perfectly accurate’ — and misidentifications (e.g., calling a cake ‘cupcakes’) are not automatically grounds for disqualification — only if they contradict the visual record; (e) ‘factually consistent’ is evaluated against the image — not against an external standard — and should not be used to penalize accurate but less specific descriptions; (f) multimodal_coherence does not evaluate or penalize terminology precision, linguistic style, or specificity — only hallucinations and contradictions — and should not be used to resolve ties based on terminology accuracy — preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity); (g) spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if they are visually implied by perspective or depth — even if not explicitly labeled — and ‘conservative inference’ does not apply to clearly implied spatial relationships — and must not penalize spatial claims that are logically implied by the image’s structure — even if not perfectly explicit. The criterion must also explicitly: (h) reward contextually grounded inferences — including flavor, texture, or composition — when visually supported — even if not explicitly labeled; (i) clarify that ‘flatly placed’ is not a misrepresentation if it accurately describes spatial arrangement; (j) remove or clarify the penalization of ‘unsupported speculation’ to avoid penalizing plausible, visually grounded inferences — and must explicitly define ‘unsupported speculation’ as fabricating non-existent visual attributes (e.g., ‘matcha flavored’ if no visual cue exists) — not as reasonable interpretation of color or texture; (k) emphasize that spatial descriptions (like ‘flatly placed’) are not hallucinations unless they contradict the visual record — and must explicitly warn against penalizing accurate, non-hallucinated descriptions of position or orientation; (l) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not applicable to factually inconsistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) when foundational criteria are violated — to avoid misapplication in cases where one answer is disqualified; (m) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and emphasize that it is only for evaluating internal consistency among factually consistent answers; (n) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, specificity, completeness) — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent; (o) explicitly distinguish between ‘visual misrepresentation’ (contradicting verifiable visual evidence) and ‘contextually misleading’ or ‘structurally surprising’ descriptions — and must not penalize accurate descriptions of static, structural features — even if they are not ‘normal’ or ‘standard’; (p) explicitly define ‘internal contradiction’ as a misrepresentation of visual evidence — not as any inference that contradicts a definitive visual cue — and must clarify that cautious, contextually grounded inferences are not penalized — even if they contradict a definitive visual cue — as long as they are grounded in the visual record; (q) explicitly allow and reward contextually grounded inferences that are visually plausible — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they do not contradict the visual record; (r) explicitly state that negative claims (e.g., ‘no one is wearing jerseys’) are not penalized under ‘internal contradiction’ — as long as they are visually supported and contextually plausible; Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer must not invent or exaggerate visual details not present in the image. For example, claiming a person is holding a phone when none is visible, or describing a background object that doesn’t exist — such details are considered hallucinations and reduce quality.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked. If the question asks about composition, an answer focusing on the animal’s mood is off-topic. Annotators check whether the answer targets the core intent of the question, not tangential or irrelevant information.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or direct visual contradictions is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically required to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly necessary to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, posture, motion, or contextually grounded actions). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all semantically essential visual components — not all visible details, nor aesthetic descriptors, nor speculative inferences — and omission of clearly visible, semantically essential elements (e.g., posture when asked ‘what is the person doing?’) is penalized. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or contextually unsupported details (e.g., ‘a camel’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant to answering the question — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question’s literal intent. If two answers are factually consistent, the one that includes more semantically essential, visually present elements wins — but only if those elements are not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to override factual consistency — factual consistency is the non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates the granularity and precision of visually verifiable details in an answer — including object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual elements — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation entirely, and no comparison should be made under this criterion. Specificity rewards answers that add accurate, non-hallucinated, granular details — even minor or non-essential ones — as long as they are visually verifiable and do not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral or environmental inferences (e.g., ‘waiting for their turn’ from posture, ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. However, it DOES penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’, ‘mirror effect’) that lacks visual grounding — as these are subjective and not descriptive of visual elements. Specificity does not reward speculative inferences — but does reward inclusion of verifiable, granular details like ‘a browser window’ — even if the action (e.g., ‘browsing’) is inferred. Hallucinations (fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible) are always penalized — even if highly detailed — and disqualify the answer from specificity evaluation. Specificity is not a tiebreaker — it applies only to factually consistent and visually grounded answers, and preference must be determined using foundational criteria (visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image) first. It is not about linguistic creativity or detail quantity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present and factually correct. Annotators should prioritize accurate, granular descriptions over vague or generic ones — but only if they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity must not override or compensate for violations of visual grounding or factual consistency — granularity is irrelevant if the answer is hallucinated or misrepresents the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative detail — and specificity is not applicable. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized — it is a hallucination. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if not central. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity is evaluated only after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is never applied to hallucinated or factually inconsistent answers. Additionally, specificity does not apply to artistic, abstract, or stylized visual elements — such as ‘pattern design’, ‘arc’, or ‘composition’ — unless they are visually verifiable or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues. Descriptive aesthetic terms (e.g., ‘eye-catching’) are only allowed if they are visually grounded — and must not be penalized for being non-essential. Contextually grounded inferences are rewarded if visually supported — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they are plausible and not hallucinated. Specificity is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded answers — and such answers must be disqualified from the entire preference comparison before any criterion evaluation. Finally, specificity rewards the most accurate, visually verifiable description — not the most semantically labeled one — and penalizes any answer that uses a semantic label (e.g., ‘logo’) that is not visually verifiable — while rewarding the answer that provides the most precise visual description — even if it uses descriptive terms (e.g., ‘human-shaped pattern’).

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should reflect confidence appropriately. If the image is ambiguous, the answer should indicate uncertainty (e.g., “possibly” or “likely”) without overstating certainty. Annotators penalize overconfidence in uncertain situations and reward humility when appropriate.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be written in simple, grammatically correct, and unambiguous language. Jargon, overly complex phrasing, or unclear syntax reduce clarity and accessibility. Annotators prefer answers that are easy to understand without requiring interpretation.

all_criteria.name: logical_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be internally coherent and free from contradictions. For example, if it says an animal is both “calm” and “in pain,” or that objects are “on opposite sides” while also “centered,” it lacks logical consistency. Annotators evaluate whether the answer’s internal logic aligns with the visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates the reasonableness of behavioral, emotional, or contextual inferences about living beings (humans, animals, or plants) — such as ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’, ‘leaning forward’, ‘waiting’, or ‘content’ — based solely on direct, unambiguous visual cues (e.g., facial expression, posture, gaze, motion blur, physical contact). It is ONLY applicable when the answer is already factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — and must be applied strictly as a tiebreaker between two factually consistent and visually grounded answers. If either visual grounding or factual consistency is violated, the answer is disqualified from plausibility evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image). Plausibility does not apply to non-living subjects (e.g., logos, statues, abstract art, inanimate objects) — and workers must report ‘inapplicable’ when the subject is non-living. It also does not apply to spatial or structural claims (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’, ‘on a shelf’) — which are evaluated under visual_grounding — nor to material, functional, or design claims (e.g., ‘made of metal’, ‘has a logo’, ‘on a laptop’) — which are evaluated under factual_consistency_with_the_image. Plausibility is NOT a disqualification tool — and must never be used to override visual grounding, factual consistency, or to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers. It does not penalize subjective or contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., ‘serious’, ‘playful’, ‘arrogant’) — as long as they are visually grounded — and must not be used to penalize plausible, posture-based inferences even if they seem contextually ‘off’ — e.g., ‘leaning forward’ is acceptable if posture supports it, even if the context seems odd. It does not evaluate descriptive style, completeness, specificity, or accuracy of terminology — only whether the inferred behavior or context is biologically or physically reasonable given the visual evidence — and must never be used to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative inference — and plausibility is not applicable. The goal is to reward accurate, visually grounded inferences that are contextually reasonable — and penalize only falsehoods or hallucinations — not subjective interpretations or minimalism. Annotators must reject any inference that contradicts the visual record — even if it seems ‘reasonable’ — and must avoid using plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. This criterion is strictly for behavioral or contextual inferences — not literal visual descriptions (e.g., ‘man holding woman’s hand’) — which are factually consistent if visually supported — and not for spatial or structural claims — which are evaluated under visual_grounding. Plausibility does not override visual grounding — and if a spatial claim is visually supported, it is not a hallucination — even if contextually ambiguous. The criterion must not be applied to non-living subjects — and must explicitly warn workers not to apply it to non-living subjects — even if they describe behavior or context — and must require workers to report ‘inapplicable’ when the subject is non-living. It must also explicitly state that it is not a preference rule — and must never be used to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers — which must be disqualified under other criteria. Plausibility is not applicable to questions asking for factual or structural claims — and workers must defer to visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image for such claims. Finally, the criterion must explicitly clarify that it is not a filter for environmental context — and that environmental claims should be evaluated under other criteria — to prevent misapplication.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
all_criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates whether an answer’s internal claims — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, postures, and inferred states — are logically consistent with each other, but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either factual consistency or visual grounding is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and preference must be determined by other foundational criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image). This criterion is NOT a tiebreaker and does NOT penalize hallucinations or misidentifications — those are handled by foundational criteria. It rewards answers that avoid internal contradictions (e.g., describing an object as ‘on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path) — but does NOT penalize plausible, contextually grounded inferences that are visually supported — even if not explicitly visible. It also does NOT penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) as long as it does not imply hallucinated visual attributes. It evaluates only visual fidelity and internal consistency — not linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or specificity. Annotators must: (1) first confirm factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from all criteria — and multimodal_coherence is inapplicable; (2) check for contradictions between claims (e.g., posture vs. action); (3) verify that inferences are grounded in observable cues (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ from posture, not ‘browsing Apple web pages’ unless Apple logos are visible); (4) penalize only when a claim misrepresents the visual record — not when it is speculative or contextually reasonable. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer internal contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after confirming factual consistency. Spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if visually implied by perspective or depth — and posture-based inferences (e.g., ‘wiping hair from head’) are rewarded as conservative, visually supported inferences — not penalized as speculation. Emotional or behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’) are not hallucinations if visually supported — and should not be penalized for being subjective or interpretive. Aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — as long as it does not imply hallucinations. The criterion applies ONLY to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and any answer with factual errors is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation, regardless of internal consistency. It is NOT applicable to static, non-motion-related questions — and should not be used to override visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer should use calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’) — not speculative reconstruction — and multimodal_coherence should not penalize this. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, vague, or overly specific — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions — not plausible, contextually grounded inferences. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must never apply multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or make conservative inferences. The criterion must explicitly state: (a) ‘conservative inference’ applies only to ambiguous visual cues — not to clear, observable behaviors — and must not penalize accurate emotional or behavioral descriptions when they are visually grounded; (b) ‘unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details or plausible, contextually grounded inferences; (c) ‘visual misrepresentation’ applies only to claims that contradict verifiable visual evidence — not to plausible, contextually grounded inferences or spatial relationships inferred from perspective; (d) ‘factually consistent’ means claims are supported by the image’s visual record — not that they are ‘visually identical’ or ‘perfectly accurate’ — and misidentifications (e.g., calling a cake ‘cupcakes’) are not automatically grounds for disqualification — only if they contradict the visual record; (e) ‘factually consistent’ is evaluated against the image — not against an external standard — and should not be used to penalize accurate but less specific descriptions; (f) multimodal_coherence does not evaluate or penalize terminology precision, linguistic style, or specificity — only hallucinations and contradictions — and should not be used to resolve ties based on terminology accuracy — preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity); (g) spatial relationships (e.g., ‘behind’, ‘in front of’) are not hallucinations if they are visually implied by perspective or depth — even if not explicitly labeled — and ‘conservative inference’ does not apply to clearly implied spatial relationships — and must not penalize spatial claims that are logically implied by the image’s structure — even if not perfectly explicit. The criterion must also explicitly: (h) reward contextually grounded inferences — including flavor, texture, or composition — when visually supported — even if not explicitly labeled; (i) clarify that ‘flatly placed’ is not a misrepresentation if it accurately describes spatial arrangement; (j) remove or clarify the penalization of ‘unsupported speculation’ to avoid penalizing plausible, visually grounded inferences — and must explicitly define ‘unsupported speculation’ as fabricating non-existent visual attributes (e.g., ‘matcha flavored’ if no visual cue exists) — not as reasonable interpretation of color or texture; (k) emphasize that spatial descriptions (like ‘flatly placed’) are not hallucinations unless they contradict the visual record — and must explicitly warn against penalizing accurate, non-hallucinated descriptions of position or orientation; (l) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not applicable to factually inconsistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) when foundational criteria are violated — to avoid misapplication in cases where one answer is disqualified; (m) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and emphasize that it is only for evaluating internal consistency among factually consistent answers; (n) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, specificity, completeness) — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent; (o) explicitly distinguish between ‘visual misrepresentation’ (contradicting verifiable visual evidence) and ‘contextually misleading’ or ‘structurally surprising’ descriptions — and must not penalize accurate descriptions of static, structural features — even if they are not ‘normal’ or ‘standard’; (p) explicitly define ‘internal contradiction’ as a misrepresentation of visual evidence — not as any inference that contradicts a definitive visual cue — and must clarify that cautious, contextually grounded inferences are not penalized — even if they contradict a definitive visual cue — as long as they are grounded in the visual record; (q) explicitly allow and reward contextually grounded inferences that are visually plausible — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they do not contradict the visual record; (r) explicitly state that negative claims (e.g., ‘no one is wearing jerseys’) are not penalized under ‘internal contradiction’ — as long as they are visually supported and contextually plausible; (s) explicitly reward conservative, depth-based spatial inferences like ‘behind’ — which are visually supported — and must explicitly penalize claims like ‘in front of’ — which are hallucinated spatial relationships — unless clearly depicted; (t) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is only applicable to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and that if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation — not penalized or evaluated under this criterion; (u) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and clarify that any candidate with factual errors is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and that the worker should defer to other criteria for comparison; (v) explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference should be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) if the candidates are factually consistent and visually grounded — and that the criterion should not be used to penalize factual errors or misidentifications; (w) explicitly distinguish between literal physical motion (which requires visual evidence like motion blur or posture) and compositional or stylistic implications (which are acceptable if visually supported) — and must clarify that descriptions of implied action — such as ‘drawing an arc’ — are not hallucinations if they are consistent with the visual composition and do not contradict the scene’s structure; (x) explicitly state that ‘drawing an arc’ or ‘implied motion’ is allowed as long as it is grounded in visual composition — and must not penalize such descriptions as hallucinations unless they contradict the visual record; (y) explicitly prohibit using factual consistency to override visual grounding — and clarify that compositional interpretations are not hallucinations if they are contextually grounded and visually supported; (z) include guidance to treat stylistic or symbolic representations (e.g., ‘drawing an arc’) as non-hallucinated if they are consistent with the visual composition — and must not penalize them as factual inconsistencies. Additionally, the criterion must explicitly: (aa) state that aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — even if it appears to contradict a spatial description — as long as it is visually grounded and does not misrepresent the visual record; (ab) clarify that multimodal_coherence does not penalize internal contradictions between aesthetic and spatial descriptors — and should instead reward descriptive accuracy and visual fidelity; (ac) include examples of coexisting descriptors (e.g., ‘arranged in a line’ + ‘messy’) to prevent misapplication; (ad) explicitly state that the criterion does not penalize accurate, contextually grounded aesthetic descriptions — even if they seem to contradict spatial claims — and must be applied only after verifying factual consistency and visual grounding — not to override or penalize aesthetic interpretations. Finally, the criterion must explicitly: (ae) state that multimodal_coherence is not a substitute for factual_consistency_with_the_image — and that workers must first verify factual consistency before applying this criterion — and (af) explicitly warn against applying multimodal_coherence to factually inconsistent answers — and clarify that any candidate with factual errors is disqualified from all criteria — including multimodal_coherence — and that the worker should defer to other criteria for comparison. The criterion must also explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is not a tiebreaker — and that preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding or specificity) — not by multimodal_coherence — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence is only a tool for evaluating internal consistency — not for resolving preference. The criterion must also clarify that when multiple factually consistent answers exist, preference must be determined by other criteria — not by multimodal_coherence — and that multimodal_coherence should not be applied to factually inconsistent answers — even if they are visually grounded or internally coherent. The criterion must also explicitly state that it does not evaluate or compare factually consistent answers — and that preference must be determined by other criteria — such as visual_grounding, specificity, or completeness — when multiple factually consistent answers exist — and that multimodal_coherence is only a tool for evaluating internal consistency — not for resolving preference.
